title: Streaming Data Specialty Exam
description: 20 questions drawn from a pool of 40, covering streaming concepts and the PDI streaming pattern across MQTT, Kafka, and AMQP. Pass mark is 80%. Open-book — browse any page, hover glossary terms, or ask the AI assistant. Your answers are saved as you go. Explanations appear after submission.

questions.scenario: A retailer loads its till transactions into the warehouse every night. It now wants a fraud alert within seconds of a suspicious card payment.
questions.prompt: What has to change about how the pipeline runs?
options: It reads the same table with a much shorter query timeout
It runs the nightly load hourly, which makes it streaming
It ends after each payment and the next payment restarts it
It stays running and handles each event as it arrives
questions.explanation: Batch works on a bounded dataset and ends when the data is exhausted; streaming works on an unbounded sequence of events, and the transformation stays running, waiting for the next one, with latency of seconds or less. An hourly load is still batch, with latency of minutes to hours. A query timeout changes nothing about when data is read. A streaming transformation is not restarted per event; it keeps running.

questions.scenario: Messages arrive one at a time, but the lookup and database write that follow are far cheaper done for a group of messages than for each one.
questions.prompt: How does the PDI streaming pattern provide that?
options: A job loops over the topic and runs a transformation once for each message
The broker groups the messages and delivers whole batches to the consumer
The consumer batches messages and hands each batch to a child transformation
The consumer emits one row per message into its own transformation's stream
questions.explanation: A parent transformation holds the consumer step, which collects messages into batches; each batch goes to a child transformation that processes it like any other PDI stream. Emitting a row per message into the same transformation gives up the batching. A job running a transformation per message pays the per-message cost the scenario wants to avoid. The batching is done by PDI's consumer step, not by the broker.

questions.scenario: A developer places Get records from stream after a Select values step in a child transformation, to add streamed rows to rows already flowing there.
questions.prompt: What should they do instead?
options: Keep it there, and set the consumer's Number of records to 1
Put it first, and bring the other rows in with a join step
Keep it there, and give Select values a batch size to pass on
Replace it with a second consumer step inside the child
questions.explanation: Get records from stream produces rows, so it must be the first step in the child transformation; to add streamed data to an existing stream, join it in with a join step. Select values has no batch size to pass on. A batch of one record does not change where a row-producing step may sit. The consumer step belongs in the parent; the child receives its batches.

questions.scenario: A consumer has Duration (ms) set to 5000 and Number of records set to 100. Its topic produces about one message per second.
questions.prompt: What does each batch sent to the child typically hold?
options: One hundred records, as the record count must always be met
One record, as each message triggers a batch of its own
About five records, but only once 100 have also arrived
About five, as the five-second window is reached first
questions.explanation: A batch is flushed when the first of the two thresholds is reached; at one message a second, five seconds pass long before 100 records arrive, so a batch carries about five. The record count is one of two triggers, not a requirement. The thresholds are alternatives, so the batch does not also wait for 100. Messages are collected into batches, not passed on one at a time.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Streaming Specialty: Kafka Use Cases

questions.scenario: Battery-powered sensors on patchy cellular links publish a reading every few seconds. Separately, a high-volume order stream must be read by three teams independently, each able to go back over recent days.
questions.prompt: Which protocols suit the two feeds?
options: MQTT for the sensors and Kafka for the order stream
MQTT for both, since one protocol is simpler to run
Kafka for the sensors and MQTT for the order stream
AMQP for both, since only it keeps messages durably
questions.explanation: MQTT needs minimal resources and suits constrained devices on unreliable links; Kafka stores streams in a distributed commit log, and each consumer tracks its own offset in it, so teams read independently and can re-read. Swapping them puts the heavy platform on the small devices and the lightweight protocol on the high-volume, multi-reader stream. One protocol for both ignores what each feed needs. AMQP queues can be durable, but Kafka is durable too, and its log is what lets several teams re-read the same stream.

questions.scenario: A second team wants its own feed of events that a producer already publishes to a topic. The producing team has no time to change anything.
questions.prompt: Why does publish/subscribe let that go ahead?
options: The broker edits the producer's settings to add the new subscriber
The producer publishes to a topic without knowing who subscribes
The new team is added to the producer's own list of recipients
The broker splits the topic so that each team gets half the events
questions.explanation: Publishers send to a topic on the broker, and any number of subscribers can register interest in that topic; the producer neither knows nor cares how many there are. The broker does not edit producers. There is no recipient list on the producer, which is the coupling publish/subscribe removes. Every subscriber to a topic receives its messages; the broker does not divide them between teams.

questions.scenario: A consumer falls behind a fast topic, and its memory use climbs until the transformation fails.
questions.prompt: Which two consumer settings bound that load?
options: Number of records per batch
Clean session on the connection
Message prefetch limit
Maximum concurrent batches
Duration (ms) for each batch
questions.explanation: These are the backpressure controls: the message prefetch limit caps how many messages PDI queues in memory, and maximum concurrent batches caps how many batches run at once (raising it adds throughput and resource use). Duration (ms) and Number of records decide when a batch is sent, not how much may queue up. Clean session decides whether an MQTT broker keeps a client's state between connections.

questions.scenario: A manufacturer is choosing a protocol for thousands of small microcontroller sensors, and power use and unit cost must stay low.
questions.prompt: Why is MQTT the usual choice?
options: It keeps every device's full history on the broker indefinitely
It encrypts every message in the device's own hardware
It guarantees exactly-once delivery whatever the settings
It needs minimal resources, so small microcontrollers run it
questions.explanation: MQTT is a lightweight protocol that small microcontrollers can run, which keeps power consumption and manufacturing cost low. A broker keeps at most one retained message per topic, not a device's history. Delivery guarantees depend on the QoS level chosen; exactly once is only QoS 2. Its appeal is the light footprint, not encryption done in device hardware.

questions.scenario: One feed sends a temperature reading every second, and losing the odd reading is harmless. Another sends payment commands, where a duplicate would charge a customer twice.
questions.prompt: Which QoS levels fit the two feeds?
options: QoS 0 for the readings and QoS 2 for the payment commands
QoS 2 for both, since the highest level is always the safest
QoS 1 for both, since it always arrives and never repeats
QoS 2 for the readings and QoS 0 for the payment commands
questions.explanation: The rule is the lowest level that satisfies the use case: QoS 0 (at most once) suits high-frequency readings where a dropped one does not matter, and QoS 2 (exactly once) is for messages where a duplicate would cause harm. Swapping them pays for a handshake on the readings and risks losing payments. QoS 1 always arrives but may be duplicated, which is exactly the payment risk. QoS 2 everywhere spends round-trips and resources the readings do not need.

questions.scenario: A team proposes taking its HiveMQ broker to production as configured, after changing the Control Center's default admin password.
questions.prompt: What is the fairest assessment of the proposal?
options: Enough, once the websocket listener moves back to port 9000
Not enough: any MQTT client can still connect with full rights
Enough: the new password closes the broker to outside clients
Not enough: every client must also be moved to QoS 2 first
questions.explanation: That deployment has no authentication or authorization: the hivemq-allow-all extension lets any MQTT client connect with full permissions, so production needs a security extension in its place. The Control Center password protects the web console, not the MQTT listener. The websocket port only avoids a clash with MinIO; it has nothing to do with security. QoS is a delivery guarantee, not an access control.

questions.scenario: An MQTT producer and consumer both show as connected in the EMQX Dashboard, but the child transformation never runs and no output files appear.
questions.prompt: Which two settings should be checked first?
options: That both clients use one and the same Client ID
That Duration (ms) or Number of records is above 0
That the Dashboard's default admin password was changed
That the consumer's QoS has been raised to 2
That producer and consumer use the same topic
questions.explanation: No output with both clients connected usually means a topic mismatch, so nothing reaches the consumer, or a batch with no trigger above zero, so no batch is ever sent to the child. The Client ID must be unique on the broker, not shared. QoS 2 changes the delivery guarantee, not whether a batch is sent. The Dashboard password governs the web console, not message flow.

questions.scenario: A sensor drops off the network for minutes at a time. QoS 1 messages published to it while it is away must reach it when it reconnects.
questions.prompt: Which connection setting does the sensor need?
options: The retained flag on each message published to it
Clean session false, so the broker keeps its state
A shorter keep-alive, so the broker notices sooner
Clean session true, so each reconnect starts afresh
questions.explanation: With a persistent session (clean session false) the broker stores the client's subscriptions and queues QoS 1 and 2 messages while it is offline, delivering them on reconnect. Clean session true discards subscriptions and queued messages at disconnect. A shorter keep-alive detects the drop sooner but queues nothing. A retained message is a single last-known value per topic, not a queue of everything missed.

questions.scenario: A pipeline raises alerts from truck telemetry as messages arrive. When one truck's transmitter fails completely, it stops publishing, and no alert is raised.
questions.prompt: What would let the pipeline learn that the truck has gone?
options: QoS 2 on the telemetry, so the missing messages are resent
A Last Will each truck registers, which the broker publishes
A retained message on the telemetry topic, read as an alert
A lower alert threshold, so a missing reading counts as zero
questions.explanation: The consumer reacts only to messages, and a silent truck sends none. A will registered at connect is published by the broker when the client drops ungracefully or misses its keep-alive, typically offline on a status topic, which a subscriber can act on. A missing reading is not a zero; no message arrives at all. QoS governs delivery of messages that were sent, and none were. A retained message holds the last value, so it would still show the truck's last reading.

questions.scenario: An operations team runs Kafka with a separate ZooKeeper ensemble and is weighing a move to KRaft mode.
questions.prompt: What does KRaft change for them?
options: Each topic's partitions are merged into a single log
Every broker must also run a Schema Registry
A second ZooKeeper ensemble is added for redundancy
Metadata moves into Kafka itself, so ZooKeeper goes
questions.explanation: KRaft consolidates metadata management inside Kafka, with the controller embedded in the broker and Raft for consensus, so there is no external ZooKeeper to run. It removes ZooKeeper rather than adding more. Partitions are unchanged. Schema Registry is a separate component, not part of Apache Kafka and not required by KRaft.

questions.scenario: A Kafka consumer restarts after a crash and carries on from where it stopped, instead of reprocessing the whole topic.
questions.prompt: What makes that possible?
options: A replay that skips records the consumer has seen
Its committed offset, its place in each partition
Removal of each message as soon as it has been read
A lock the broker holds on each unread message
questions.explanation: The offset is a sequential id that identifies a record within a partition; the consumer commits its offset and resumes from it. Kafka holds no per-message lock. It keeps messages in its log rather than deleting them on read, which is why several consumers can read the same data. A replay that skipped seen records would still reread the whole topic.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Streaming Specialty: Kafka Use Cases

questions.scenario: A new consumer group is pointed at a long-running topic and at once processes months of old messages, which nobody expected.
questions.prompt: What explains it?
options: No committed offset, and auto.offset.reset is earliest
The topic's retention had expired, forcing a full replay
The consumer committed offset zero on its very first poll
A new group replays the whole topic whatever its settings
questions.explanation: auto.offset.reset sets where to start when there is no committed offset to resume from, which is the case for a brand-new group; earliest starts at the beginning, latest would have taken only new messages. A new group follows that setting, so it does not always replay. Expired retention removes old messages rather than replaying them. Committing offset zero is a consequence of starting at the beginning, not its cause.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Streaming Specialty: Kafka Use Cases

questions.scenario: Loading a Kafka stream into MySQL, index creation fails with BLOB/TEXT column 'user_id' used in key specification without a key length.
questions.prompt: What fixes it in the child transformation?
options: Changing Table output's commit size from 1000 down to 1
Running the ALTER TABLE ... TINYTEXT that the SQL button offers
Mapping event_id so that MySQL has a key it can index
Setting each string's length on Select values' Metadata tab
questions.explanation: Without explicit lengths PDI maps String fields to TINYTEXT, which MySQL cannot index; lengths on the Select values Metadata tab make PDI generate VARCHAR. The SQL button's ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY user_id TINYTEXT makes the problem permanent, so close it without executing. Commit size controls how often rows are committed, not column types. event_id is an AUTO_INCREMENT key MySQL fills itself and must not be mapped.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Streaming Specialty: Kafka Use Cases

questions.scenario: A child transformation must turn register_time_epoch, in epoch milliseconds, into seconds for a MySQL TIMESTAMP column.
questions.prompt: Why is a Formula step used rather than a Calculator step?
options: MySQL rejects the values that a Calculator step produces
Formula takes a constant like 1000; Calculator needs two fields
Calculator cannot return an Integer result from a division
Formula runs faster than Calculator on batches of streamed rows
questions.explanation: Calculator requires both operands to be existing stream fields, so a literal 1000 cannot be entered; Formula accepts [register_time_epoch] / 1000 directly. Calculator's result type is not the limitation. Speed is not the reason given. MySQL receives a number either way; the issue is building the expression, not the value.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Streaming Specialty: Kafka Use Cases

questions.scenario: A Table output step writing to MySQL's kafka_warehouse database has kafka_warehouse typed into its Target schema field, and the step fails.
questions.prompt: What is the fix?
options: Switch the connection's access type from Native to ODBC
Leave Target schema blank, as the connection names the database
Type the table as kafka_warehouse.user_events in Target table
Set the commit size to 1 so that each row is checked on its own
questions.explanation: MySQL takes the database from the connection; a Target schema makes PDI qualify the table as kafka_warehouse.user_events, which can fail. Typing that qualified name into Target table recreates the same problem. Commit size does not affect how the table is named. The access type is not the cause; Native JDBC is what the connection uses.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Streaming Specialty: Kafka Use Cases

questions.scenario: A topic with four partitions is read by a consumer group of two. Throughput falls short, and a colleague proposes running eight consumers.
questions.prompt: What will eight consumers achieve?
options: Nothing, as group size has no effect on how partitions are read
Duplicate processing, as all eight share every partition
About four times the throughput, as each reads every partition
At most four will work, as each partition goes to one member
questions.explanation: Each consumer in a group is assigned a subset of the topic's partitions, and a partition goes to one member, so four partitions keep at most four consumers busy and the rest sit idle; more throughput needs more partitions. Consumers in a group do not each read every partition. Group size does matter, up to the partition count. Members split the partitions rather than sharing them, so nothing is processed twice.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Streaming Specialty: Kafka Use Cases

questions.scenario: Room sensors publish readings that must reach a tv_room queue on a RabbitMQ broker.
questions.prompt: What decides which queue a published message lands in?
options: The producer, which writes into the queue's storage directly
The broker, which spreads messages evenly over all its queues
The exchange, through its bindings and the routing key
The consumer, which pulls any message from any queue it likes
questions.explanation: A producer sends to an exchange, never directly to a queue, and the exchange routes using bindings (links between it and queues) and the routing key; the sensor script publishes to the default exchange with routing key tv_room. The producer does not write into queues. Consumers read from the queue they are given; they do not choose messages. The broker does not spread messages evenly; routing follows bindings.

questions.scenario: Every message must reach three queues. A colleague proposes a topic exchange with a wildcard binding instead of a fanout exchange.
questions.prompt: What is the fairest assessment of the proposal?
options: They are equivalent, so the choice is purely a matter of style
Fanout fits better: it broadcasts to all bound queues, ignoring keys
Topic fits better: a wildcard can be narrowed later with no change
Neither works, since three queues need three separate exchanges
questions.explanation: A fanout exchange broadcasts every message to all bound queues and ignores routing keys, which is exactly the requirement; the wildcard version works but makes every message's routing key part of the contract for no benefit. Narrowing later is a future requirement, not today's. The two are not equivalent: one depends on routing keys and one does not. One exchange can be bound to any number of queues.

questions.scenario: A queue must keep its messages through a broker restart and must be usable by more than one connection over its life.
questions.prompt: How should it be declared?
options: Durable, and neither exclusive nor auto-delete
Durable and exclusive, so one consumer owns it
Transient, with auto-delete so it never goes stale
Transient, exclusive and auto-delete
questions.explanation: A durable queue is saved to disk and survives broker restarts; leaving out exclusive lets more than one connection use it, and leaving out auto-delete stops it vanishing when its consumers disconnect. Transient queues do not survive a restart. An exclusive queue is used by one connection and deleted when that connection closes. Auto-delete removes the queue when its consumer count drops to zero.

questions.scenario: A developer starts a producer that publishes several hundred messages to a new exchange, then starts the AMQP Consumer step. The consumer connects without error but receives none of those messages.
questions.prompt: What happened to the messages?
options: Buffered by the producer until a consumer sent an acknowledgement
Stored in a default queue the consumer was not bound to
Lost, as no queue was bound until the consumer created one
Held by the exchange until a queue was bound, then delivered
questions.explanation: Exchanges route and queues store; the consumer step creates its queue and binding, which is why it should run first, before messages are produced. Until then the exchange had nowhere to route them. An exchange holds nothing itself. There was no queue bound for the messages to wait in. The producer had already published them; it keeps no buffer waiting for consumers.

questions.scenario: A queue feeds a consumer that runs once a night. A colleague proposes declaring the queue auto-delete, so that no stale queues are left between runs.
questions.prompt: What is the fairest assessment of the proposal?
options: Accept it, with exclusive added so the consumer recreates it
Accept it: auto-delete removes a queue only on broker restart
Reject it: an auto-delete queue cannot be bound to an exchange
Reject it: the queue would vanish as each night's run ends
questions.explanation: Auto-delete removes a queue when its consumer count drops to zero, which happens every time the nightly run finishes, so everything published before the next run has no queue to wait in; a durable queue is the right call. A broker restart is what removes transient queues, not what triggers auto-delete. Exclusive deletes the queue when its connection closes, so it makes the loss worse. Auto-delete queues can be bound; binding is not the problem.

questions.scenario: An AMQP Consumer step names an existing queue that another application declared non-durable. The step itself would create a durable queue.
questions.prompt: What happens when the transformation runs?
options: It reads from the queue and ignores the difference
It creates a second queue with a numeric suffix added
It changes the existing queue to durable and carries on
It aborts, as the queue exists with other settings
questions.explanation: The step creates a new queue (durable, not auto-delete, not exclusive) only on first run; if a queue of that name already exists with different settings, the transformation aborts. It does not alter another application's queue. It does not create a renamed copy. It does not ignore the mismatch, which is why the abort happens.

questions.scenario: A team will rebuild a nightly load as a streaming pipeline and wants to keep the parsing and table-loading steps it already trusts. A colleague says streaming in PDI means learning a new set of steps.
questions.prompt: What is the fairest assessment of the colleague's view?
options: Right: each protocol needs its own set of processing steps after it
Mostly wrong: the consumer and Get records from stream are the new parts
Mostly wrong: nothing is new, as the batch transformation runs as is
Right: streaming transformations use their own separate set of steps
questions.explanation: Every streaming source follows one parent/child pattern: only the consumer step at the front changes, and the child starts with Get records from stream; after that, JSON Input, Select values, Formula and Table output work as in any transformation. Streaming does not have its own processing steps. The same processing steps serve every protocol. The batch transformation does not run unchanged: it needs a consumer in a parent and Get records from stream at its start.

questions.scenario: Robots publish to industrial/robot/sensor, industrial/arm/sensor and industrial/press/sensor. One MQTT Consumer must take all three topics and nothing else under industrial/.
questions.prompt: Which topic should it subscribe to?
options: +/sensor/#
industrial/*/sensor
industrial/+/sensor
industrial/#
questions.explanation: + matches exactly one level, so industrial/+/sensor matches the three sensor topics and nothing else. # matches everything under industrial/, which is more than wanted. * is not an MQTT wildcard. +/sensor/# needs sensor as the second level, which these topics do not have.

questions.scenario: A dashboard subscribes to industrial/robot/status an hour after a robot came online. The robot published online to that topic once, when it connected.
questions.prompt: Why does the dashboard see online straight away?
options: QoS 1 makes the broker resend it until each client acks
The robot republishes online whenever anyone subscribes
The broker sends every message of the last hour on subscribe
The message was retained, so the broker replays it
questions.explanation: A message published with the retained flag is stored as the topic's last-known value and delivered at once to any client that subscribes later. Publishers do not see who subscribes, so the robot cannot republish on demand. A broker keeps one retained message per topic, not an hour of history. QoS 1 re-sends a message until it is acknowledged by the clients subscribed when it was sent, not to later ones.

questions.scenario: To test a sensor's Last Will, a developer stops the sensor script by calling disconnect(), then waits several minutes. The status topic never changes to offline.
questions.prompt: Why did the will not fire?
options: A will fires only after ten keep-alive intervals have passed
A graceful disconnect tells the broker to discard the will
A will is sent to the sensor itself when it next connects
A will can only be published to a topic with no retained value
questions.explanation: The will is for an unexpected drop: a crash, network loss or missed keep-alive. Calling disconnect() is a graceful disconnect, which tells the broker to discard the will, so nothing is published; killing the process would test it. The broker acts after 1.5 times the keep-alive, not ten intervals. Wills are commonly published retained to a status topic that already holds online. The broker publishes the will to the topic's subscribers, not to the departed client.

questions.scenario: A sensor using the client library's default keep-alive of 60 seconds is killed without disconnecting. Operators watch its status topic for the will.
questions.prompt: How long should they allow before expecting it?
options: No time at all, as the broker sees the process end
Forever, as killing the process discards the will
Up to about 90 seconds, 1.5 times the keep-alive
Exactly 60 seconds, a single keep-alive interval
questions.explanation: If the broker hears nothing within 1.5 times the keep-alive interval, it drops the client and publishes its will, so a 60-second keep-alive means up to about 90 seconds. The broker cannot see a remote process end; it notices the silence. One interval is when the client should have sent a PINGREQ, not when the broker gives up. A kill is an ungraceful drop, which is exactly when the will is sent.

questions.scenario: HiveMQ and EMQX run on the same machine. A consumer meant to read truck telemetry from EMQX connects without error but receives nothing, while the producer shows as connected in the EMQX Dashboard.
questions.prompt: What should be checked first?
options: That it connects through the Dashboard's port 18083
That its connection uses EMQX's port 1884, not 1883
That HiveMQ is stopped, since two brokers cannot coexist
That its Client ID matches the producer's Client ID
questions.explanation: HiveMQ listens on 1883 and EMQX on 1884, both at once, so a consumer on 1883 connects happily to HiveMQ and hears nothing of EMQX's topics. The two brokers are deliberately run side by side on their own ports. 18083 is EMQX's web Dashboard, not an MQTT listener. A Client ID must be unique on the broker, so it should not match the producer's.

questions.scenario: A team proposes the topic /Plant 1/Robot Sensors/Temperature for its readings, and a production monitoring client subscribed to #.
questions.prompt: Which change follows MQTT topic best practice?
options: Add a trailing # to the topic name so subscribers can match it
Drop the leading / and the spaces, and narrow the # subscription
Create the topic on the broker before anyone publishes to it
Use accented names so that each plant's topics stay distinct
questions.explanation: Topics should be short, specific and ASCII, without spaces or a leading /, and a client should not subscribe to a broad # in production. Brokers accept any valid topic on the fly, so nothing is created first. Wildcards are for subscriptions only, never part of a published topic. Non-ASCII names go against the best practice.

questions.scenario: A child transformation sometimes fails partway through writing a batch to MySQL. The team must not lose records when that happens, and reprocessing a batch is acceptable.
questions.prompt: Which Offset Management setting suits them?
options: Commit when batch completed, so a failed batch is read again
Neither, as auto.offset.reset set to latest prevents loss
Commit when record read, so each offset is saved soonest
Either, since offsets matter only when a new group starts
questions.explanation: With Commit when batch completed the offset moves only after the child has finished, so a batch that fails is read again rather than skipped. Commit when record read advances the offset before the batch is written, so a failure skips records already counted as read. Offsets are what a restarted consumer resumes from, not only a new group's concern. latest starts from new messages when there is no committed offset, which skips data rather than protecting it.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Streaming Specialty: Kafka Use Cases

questions.scenario: A warehouse table stores kafka_topic, kafka_partition and kafka_offset beside each user event loaded from Kafka.
questions.prompt: What do those three columns make possible?
options: Spotting duplicates, as together they name one record
Joining each event to the region the user registered in
Sending each event back to Kafka if the load has failed
Ordering the events by the time each user registered
questions.explanation: An offset identifies a record within its partition, so topic, partition and offset together identify one Kafka record; grouping on them and looking for counts above one finds anything loaded twice, and they also show offset progress per partition. Registration time is in register_time. The region is in region_id. Nothing in the pipeline sends events back to Kafka.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Streaming Specialty: Kafka Use Cases

questions.scenario: On a Windows machine, a Kafka Consumer step with bootstrap server localhost:9092 cannot connect, although the Kafka container is running.
questions.prompt: What should the connection use?
options: 127.0.0.1:9092, as localhost resolves to IPv6 first
The Cluster option, with a Hadoop cluster configuration
localhost:9090, the port of the broker's web console
localhost:2181, the port that ZooKeeper listens on
questions.explanation: Windows resolves localhost to IPv6 first, so the connection uses the IPv4 address 127.0.0.1:9092. 2181 is ZooKeeper's port, and a KRaft cluster has no ZooKeeper. 9090 is HiveMQ's Control Center, not Kafka. The Cluster option is for a Hadoop cluster configuration; Direct with bootstrap servers is right here.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Streaming Specialty: Kafka Use Cases

questions.scenario: Several teams produce Avro messages to shared Kafka topics. Consumers keep breaking when a producer changes the structure of its messages.
questions.prompt: Which component addresses this?
options: A consumer group, which pins the schema its members read
The KRaft controller, which validates each message's shape
A Schema Registry, a separate service both sides consult
A broker setting that rejects messages of an unknown shape
questions.explanation: A Schema Registry is a central repository for managing and validating message schemas; it sits apart from the brokers, and producers and consumers talk to it alongside Kafka to send and retrieve schemas. The controller manages cluster state and administrative tasks, not message content. Brokers store data and serve requests. A consumer group divides partitions between consumers.

questions.scenario: User events are produced without a key and land scattered across a topic's partitions. A team wants all of one user's events to go to the same partition.
questions.prompt: What should the producer change?
options: Put the user's ID into the message value's JSON
Give each user a separate consumer group
Give each message the registration time as its timestamp
Give each message the user's ID as its Kafka key
questions.explanation: The key determines how messages are distributed to partitions, and without one they are spread at random. The timestamp records when the message reached the server; it does not choose a partition. The message value is the payload, and its contents do not decide the partition. Consumer groups decide how messages are read, not where they are written.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Streaming Specialty: Kafka Use Cases

questions.scenario: An AMQP Consumer step's Exchange name is left blank. Its queue must receive only the messages published with the routing key tv_room.
questions.prompt: Which exchange does the step bind its queue to?
options: A topic exchange that matches every routing key by default
The default exchange, of type DIRECT, matching on routing key
A new fanout exchange created with the queue's name
No exchange, so the queue receives every message on the broker
questions.explanation: A blank Exchange name uses the DEFAULT exchange, of type DIRECT, which routes on the routing key; the sensor script publishes to it with routing key tv_room. The step does not invent a fanout exchange, which would ignore routing keys. Every message goes through an exchange, so a queue never receives everything on the broker. A topic exchange matches on patterns given as routing keys, not everything by default.

questions.scenario: An order service publishes to RabbitMQ, and a billing service consumes from its own queue. Billing goes down for ten minutes during a deploy.
questions.prompt: What happens to the orders placed in those ten minutes?
options: They wait in billing's queue until it is back
The broker hands them back to the order service as failed
The order service blocks until billing answers each one
They are lost, as no consumer was there to read them
questions.explanation: Queues store messages until a consumer retrieves them, which is what decouples the two services and keeps a temporary failure from losing information. Unlike messages sent to an exchange with no queue bound, these have a queue to wait in. Communication is asynchronous, so the order service does not wait for billing. The broker does not return queued messages to the producer.
